trigger_points.location_description: Belly in the middle third of the dorsal forearm emerging between extensor digitorum and extensor carpi radialis brevis, and the musculotendinous junction at the intersection point. [clinical reasoning -- no Travell & Simons figure exists for APL]
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Travell and Simons do not map an APL pattern. Experimental intramuscular hypertonic-saline injection produced referred pain to the radial aspect of the wrist in 62% of subjects, to the dorsal aspects of the middle and ring fingers in 14%, and to both in 24% -- a distribution resembling the superficial radial nerve territory and the pain of De Quervain's disease (Hwang, Kang, Shin & Kim 2005).
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Repetitive thumb abduction with radial deviation (lifting infants, texting, hammering, racquet sports). [clinical reasoning]
trigger_points.notes: Non-myofascial differential: De Quervain's disease, intersection syndrome, Wartenberg's syndrome, basal-joint and STT arthritis, scaphoid fracture or nonunion, C6 radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Hwang, Kang, Shin & Kim (2005) Am J Phys Med Rehabil 84:593-597 (experimental referred-pain mapping) -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference, which notes no distinct Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual figure exists for APL; TrP location and activation factors are labelled [clinical reasoning] there.

clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Abduction and extension of the thumb carpometacarpal joint (radial abduction), stabilizing the joint during pinch [1, 5]. At the wrist: A principal radial deviator together with ECRL, with slight wrist flexion because the tendon passes palmar to the flexion–extension axis at the radial styloid [1, 5, 6]. Carpal stability: Carpal supinator, protective for the scapholunate joint, most efficient in neutral forearm rotation; first-phase motor of the dart-throwing motion with ECRL [14, 16, 17, 19]. Importance: Dynamic stabilizer of the thumb basal joint; accessory slips are used for suspensionplasty in basal-joint arthroplasty [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: 1st compartment synovial sheath, frequently divided by a septum that places EPB in its own subcompartment (reported in roughly a third to two-thirds of wrists across anatomical and surgical series) [48]. No bursa. Relations: Branches of the superficial radial nerve cross the compartment; the radial artery lies deep in the snuffbox against the scaphoid and trapezium [1]. Coupled structures: Radial styloid groove and 1st compartment septum, superficial radial nerve, radial artery, scaphoid, trapezium, thumb basal joint and thenar muscles (accessory slips), ECRL/ECRB tendons at the intersection [1, 35, 48].

clinical.notes: De Quervain's stenosing tenosynovitis of the 1st compartment (Finkelstein and Eichhoff tests) is the commonest wrist tendinopathy; an unrecognized EPB subcompartment explains failed blind injections and incomplete releases [47, 48]. Intersection syndrome arises where the APL and EPB bellies cross the radial wrist extensors [35]. Branches of the superficial radial nerve are at risk during compartment release. Snuffbox tenderness points to the scaphoid.
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
